Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette: Mary, a 76-year-old widowed European woman and former ship captain, has been grappling with the aftermath of an encounter with police violence that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event was vividly etched into her mind; she often felt as if she were reliving it in real time, a feeling so acute that she could practically see every detail, like flipping through photographs. These intrusive memories have been relentless and piercing, making it difficult for Mary to find peace. Since the incident, Mary has thrown herself into work with an intensity bordering on obsession. She had come to believe that keeping busy was the only way to avoid the searing clarity of her traumatic memories. By working long hours and constantly focusing on tasks, she could momentarily escape from the vivid recollections of the terrifying event. This overworking behavior became a coping mechanism, one that allowed her to push away thoughts and feelings about what had happened. However, despite her efforts to distract herself with work, Mary found it increasingly difficult to shake off the haunting images and sensations from the traumatic incident. The more she tried to avoid thinking about it by burying herself in tasks, the more vividly the memories returned. Her mind would often drift back to the event during moments of quiet or when her schedule slowed down, leading to a vicious cycle where the clarity and detail of the memories seemed to intensify her need for distraction. Mary dwelled on how she used to be before the incident, a person who could navigate her ship with ease and confidence. Now, the trauma had left her feeling unmoored and disoriented, unable to find her old sense of self amidst the overwhelming intrusions. She often found herself ruminating about why this event happened to her, grappling with questions that seemed impossible to answer. The memories were so vivid that even simple triggers could set off a cascade of intrusive thoughts and sensations. For example, the sound of sirens would immediately transport Mary back to the traumatic incident, causing her heart to race and her palms to sweat. These experiences often led her to overwork further as she sought refuge in tasks to avoid confronting these memories. Despite her best efforts to keep busy, Mary began to feel the strain on both her physical and mental health. Her once-clear mind was now clouded with persistent reminders of the event, and the isolation from others only amplified this internal turmoil. She became increasingly isolated, avoiding social interactions that might remind her of the trauma or trigger distressing memories. Mary’s daily life as a ship captain had been profoundly affected. The trauma had made it challenging for her to focus on her duties without being interrupted by intrusive thoughts and sensations. Her coworkers noticed changes in her behavior, but Mary was reluctant to discuss what she was going through, fearing that others would not understand or would judge her. What finally brought Mary to seek help was a combination of exhaustion from overworking and the realization that her coping mechanisms were no longer effective. She had come to believe that there must be a better way to manage her symptoms, one that did not involve constantly pushing herself to the brink. In therapy, she expressed a deep hope for finding peace and a sense of stability once again. Mary was most afraid of losing control over her thoughts and feelings, of being perpetually haunted by memories that felt as real as they had on the day of the incident. She hoped to regain some semblance of normalcy in her daily life and work, free from the constant intrusion of traumatic recollections. With support, she believed it was possible to navigate through this difficult period and find a way forward.
